newsitem.title: CANADA: British Columbia unveils forest jobs program.
newsitem.headline: British Columbia unveils forest jobs program.

text.p: British Columbia announced a plan on Thursday aimed at adding 39,800 jobs to its forest industry by 2001.
Premier Glen Clark was due to make the announcement today in the northern community of Prince George.
According to materials distributed before his news conference, 22,400 of the increase would come from direct jobs and 17,400 from spinoff jobs.
The province's Forest Renewal British Columbia agency will spend C$300 million on silviculture and other projects, creating 5,000 direct jobs.

Major forestry companies are targeted to create 8,900 jobs. Of that amount, 3,900 would come from increased harvesting facilitated by a streamlining of government bureaucracy. Red tape has prevented companies from cutting their full allocations of wood and they face a backlog.
Another 3,000 jobs of the jobs at big forest companies would be created after negotiations with the unions on reducing overtime and hours of work for existing employees.
Local media reported that the government was willing to subsidize payrolls to maintain pay levels for workers who face shortened hours.
The remanufacturing sector is slated to add 5,000 jobs and small and medium-size forest enterprises 1,500 jobs. Programs to renew salmon streams in logging areas would add 2,000 jobs.
Clark has threatened to take away cutting rights from companies that do not participate in the program.

Government documents showed that companies who joined would have access to new timber that became available and would not face an existing penalty amounting to five percent of their harvest if they sold timber licenses.

The province has structured the plan in a way that it hopes will avoid riling the U.S. lumber industry and provoking trade tensions. U.S. producers are likely to scrutinize it carefully to ensure it contains no hidden subsidies to British Columbia firms.
